title: Global Development’s Missing Ingredient
gist: Gordon Whitman argues global development fails because of a 'crisis of agency' on the demand side of democracy: 74% of the world's population now lives in autocracies and aid is designed by agencies and foreign contractors, so he proposes an International Campaign for Integral Human Development modeled on the Catholic Campaign for Human Development, arguing that dedicating even 1% of private development financing to grassroots organizing would be transformative.

insights.claim: According to the V-Dem Institute, 74% of the global population now lives in autocracies, while people in democracies are increasingly critical of how their governments work.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: A hard baseline for political-risk modeling: the majority of global population and much of global growth now sits under autocratic governance, raising rule-of-law discounts on EM assets.
insights.quote: According to the V-Dem Institute, 74% of the global population now live in autocracies, while those fortunate to reside in democracies are increasingly critical of how their governments work.
insights.locator: According to the V-Dem Institute

insights.claim: People overwhelmingly value democracy while large majorities do not believe their elected officials care about their views, a gap that is about responsiveness rather than legitimacy of the system itself.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Explains why anti-incumbent volatility persists even where democratic support is high — expect continued electoral churn and policy discontinuity.
insights.quote: People overwhelmingly value democracy, but large majorities don’t believe that their elected officials care about their views.
insights.locator: People overwhelmingly value democracy

insights.claim: Rapid technological and cultural change combined with rising economic insecurity has eroded support for liberal institutions and fomented anti-elite sentiment across the political spectrum, not just on one side.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Anti-elite politics is bipartisan and structurally driven, so policy risk to incumbents, platforms and large institutions is not mean-reverting with any single election.
insights.quote: Rapid technological and cultural change, along with rising economic insecurity, have eroded support for liberal institutions and fomented anti-elite sentiment across the political spectrum.
insights.locator: Rapid technological and cultural change

insights.claim: The underlying problem beneath political discontent is a crisis of agency — people lack the ability to influence decisions that shape their lives — rather than a crisis of ideology or information.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Reframes populism as a demand for control, implying that policies restoring perceived agency, not just income transfers, are what defuse political risk.
insights.quote: At the heart of this discontent is a deeper problem: a crisis of agency.
insights.locator: At the heart of this discontent

insights.claim: Global development projects are typically designed by aid agencies and managed by foreign contractors and NGOs, leaving intended beneficiaries with no role in design decisions.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Structural explanation for weak aid ROI; a reason to discount headline development-finance commitments as indicators of on-the-ground outcomes.
insights.quote: projects are often designed by aid agencies and managed by foreign contractors and NGOs
insights.locator: That is certainly the case in global development

insights.claim: In 2023 the People's Ecumenical Organization for the Development of Haiti, Communities of Faith Organizing for Action in El Salvador, and Faith in Action International asked USAID to pause non-emergency work for six weeks and send staff to listen to people about the aid they wanted — and the request was not met.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that participatory reform stalls at the implementation layer even when leadership is sympathetic — a caution on 'localization' pledges from development institutions.
insights.locator: In 2023, the People’s Ecumenical Organization for the Development of Haiti

insights.claim: Then-USAID Administrator Samantha Power embraced the mission of reforming the agency but she and her staff could not fathom shifting decision-making to beneficiaries, offering only a presentation on USAID's work delivered in Terrier-Rouge.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Shows reform-minded leadership is insufficient without structural change — set low expectations for institutional self-reform absent external pressure.
insights.quote: While then-USAID Administrator Samantha Power had embraced the mission of reforming the agency, she and her staff could not fathom shifting decision-making to beneficiaries.
insights.locator: While then-USAID Administrator Samantha Power

insights.claim: Large bureaucratic institutions are unlikely to hold themselves fully accountable without outside pressure, which is why participatory budgeting, complaint mechanisms at international financial institutions, and localization initiatives have underdelivered.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: A test for any accountability reform: if the pressure is internal only, discount the promised outcomes.
insights.quote: Large bureaucratic institutions are unlikely to hold themselves fully accountable without outside pressure.
insights.locator: But, as the example of USAID in Haiti shows

insights.claim: The democracy deficit has a demand side that reform agendas ignore: millions of people need organizations through which they can collectively negotiate their interests, not just channels institutions offer them.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Identifies organizing capacity, not institutional design, as the scarce input — the place where marginal funding has the highest leverage.
insights.quote: This is the demand side of the democracy deficit: millions of people need organizations through which they can collectively negotiate their interests.
insights.locator: This is the demand side of the democracy deficit

themes.theme: The CCHD as a replicable model

insights.claim: US Catholic bishops established the Catholic Campaign for Human Development in Chicago in 1969, two years after Pope Paul VI's 1967 encyclical Populorum Progressio, to fund organizations addressing the root causes of poverty.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Establishes a 50-plus-year track record as the evidentiary base for the author's proposed global fund.
insights.locator: One model is the Catholic Campaign for Human Development

insights.claim: The CCHD's eligibility rule requires grantee organizations both to seek changes in the policies and systems that keep people in poverty and to maintain a governing board at least half of whose members are involuntarily low-income.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable governance criterion for any funder wanting accountability to beneficiaries rather than to intermediaries.
insights.quote: maintain a governing board in which at least half of the members are involuntarily low-income
insights.locator: To be eligible for a grant

insights.claim: The CCHD disburses funds based on the Catholic principle of subsidiarity — that decisions should be made closest to the people they affect — combining clear criteria with a decentralized structure to guard against top-down bureaucracy.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: The stated mechanism by which a global fund could avoid becoming another top-down aid bureaucracy; the test for evaluating similar vehicles.
insights.locator: The CCHD raises funds through an annual collection

insights.claim: Over more than 50 years the CCHD's ecosystem has produced concrete policy wins including higher wages, paid family leave, more affordable housing units, and health coverage for the uninsured.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that grassroots organizing funding translates into measurable regulatory and wage outcomes — a channel through which organized labor-adjacent groups move policy affecting employers.
insights.locator: For more than 50 years, the CCHD has been instrumental

insights.claim: Many of the most prominent local and state groups now anchoring the defense of American democracy, both secular and faith-based, began with multiyear general support grants from the CCHD.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Long-horizon, unrestricted funding, not project grants, is what produced today's civic infrastructure — relevant to how philanthropic capital should be structured.
insights.quote: many of the most prominent local and state groups, both secular and faith-based, anchoring the defense of American democracy got their start with multiyear general support grants from the CCHD
insights.locator: It has also nurtured generations of grassroots leaders

insights.claim: The author proposes an International Campaign for Integral Human Development: a global vehicle providing long-term funding to launch and scale grassroots organizations powerful enough to influence national or global policy.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
entities: International Campaign for Integral Human Development
insights.so_what: A named institutional proposal to watch; if it gains backers it would redirect development capital toward organizing rather than service delivery.
insights.locator: The world needs an equivalent mechanism

insights.claim: Dedicating even 1% of private development financing to grassroots organizing would be transformative, making the proposal a marginal reallocation rather than a demand for new money.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Low-cost, high-asymmetry ask: a 1% reallocation is within the discretion of existing funders, so adoption risk is political rather than financial.
insights.quote: dedicating even 1% of private development financing to grassroots organizing would be transformative
insights.locator: And it would be well worth the effort

insights.claim: Such a fund should draw on Catholic experience while including other faiths and secular funders who have publicly called for shifting decision-making to local communities, making it explicitly ecumenical rather than denominational.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Signals a coalition wide enough to be fundable; the constraint is governance design, not ideological alignment.
insights.locator: It could draw on Catholic experience

insights.claim: Faith-based institutions committed to human dignity and pluralism are positioned to supply not just inspiration but the organizing infrastructure that development finance lacks.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Identifies religious networks as an under-recognized distribution and governance channel in development — relevant to where institutional capital could route funds at scale.
insights.quote: not only in inspiring people to act, but also in building the infrastructure required for organizing at scale
insights.locator: Faith-based institutions committed to human dignity

themes.theme: Conflict as a precondition for change

insights.claim: Dialogue is not the absence of conflict, and without conflict there is no change — so consensus-seeking development processes structurally fail to shift power.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Explains why stakeholder-consultation models produce little: absent adversarial pressure, incumbent institutions do not move.
insights.quote: Dialogue is not the absence of conflict, but without conflict there is no change.
insights.locator: In Magnifica Humanitas, Leo describes listening and dialogue

insights.claim: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, frames two futures — top-down technocratic rule symbolized by the Tower of Babel versus bottom-up reconstruction on the Nehemiah model — and observes that most people are merely watching and waiting.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: A high-profile moral framing that could mobilize institutional Catholic capital and advocacy against technocratic and billionaire-dominated governance models.
insights.quote: most people are watching and waiting, observing from afar and merely hoping for the best
insights.locator: WASHINGTON, DC—In his first encyclical

insights.claim: In a world increasingly dominated by billionaires, bottom-up collective action appears as futile as it is commendable — yet the author argues it has been done before and the real barrier is the absence of avenues, not of will.
insights.speaker: Gordon Whitman
insights.so_what: Locates the bottleneck in organizational infrastructure rather than public appetite, which is where funding can actually move the needle.
insights.quote: In a world increasingly dominated by billionaires, the second vision of collective action seems as commendable as it is futile.
insights.locator: In a world increasingly dominated by billionaires
